title: TB9-31200
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I dismiss this appeal.

XXXX XXXX is a citizen of India from Tamil Nadu state. He alleged that he risked persecution by the police because they suspected him of supporting the LTTE (Tamil Tigers). The RPD dismissed his claim for refugee protection because it found there was not a serious possibility that he would be persecuted were he to return to India. I agree. Allegations
XXXX XXXX XXXX allegations were well summarized in his appeal memorandum:

He owned an XXXX XXXX XXXX business. He frequented a camp where Tamil refugees from Sri Lanka lived. He made friends with a man who told him about the sufferings of the Tamil population in Sri Lanka. The Appellant would take food and clothing to the camp.

He gave jobs to two young men who were inmates of the camp. They were K and J. They worked for him for nine years. J was arrested by police in XXXX 2013 because he had connections to the LTTE for whom he was believed to be collecting money, to which he apparently confessed.

The police came searching for K, who was not at the store. The police questioned the Appellant in relation to both men and accused the Appellant of supporting the LTTE. The police told the Appellant that they would continue to search for information and that if they found out anything, they would arrest the Appellant.

The Appellant contacted a member of the legislative assembly of his district who told the Appellant he could not protect the Appellant and advised the Appellant to leave India, which he did [by flying to Canada in XXXX 2014].
After the Appellant left India, the police went to his house and threatened his wife and son. The police do not know that the Appellant is in Canada.

The Appellant testified that he did not know the current situation of either J or K, and the last time he had contact with J was before J was arrested in XXXX 2013; nor has he had contact with K since that time. RPD decision

The RPD made no clear finding that the alleged events of XXXX 2013 had not occurred. It did find that XXXX XXXX XXXX delay in pursuing his refugee claim undermined the credibility of his allegation that he fled India because he feared persecution by the police. Finally, it found that he had not established a well-founded fear of future persecution because the police had only said they would arrest him if they found evidence that he supported the LTTE, but they had not found such evidence nor did it exist. Delay in pursuing refugee claim initiated upon entry to Canada - RPD correct

As Counsel notes, the delay aspect of this case is unusual. XXXX XXXX XXXX initiated his refugee claim on the day he arrived in Canada. He did not pursue it, however, for another two years and four months.
In his BOC, XXXX XXXX XXXX did not address the timing of his pursuit of his refugee claim.

The CBSA documents in evidence and XXXX XXXX XXXX testimony established that the application for a Canadian business visitor's visa that he presented in late XXXX 2013 was based on fabricated information. XXXX XXXX XXXX tried to use that visa to enter Canada.1 Canadian immigration officials at the airport in Montreal, however, denied him entry to Canada when he arrived on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014 because his visa had been obtained by misrepresentation. CBSA's records state that on that same day, shortly after being confronted with this information, he indicated he wanted to make a refugee claim.2

Although CBSA gave XXXX XXXX XXXX documents instructing him to return shortly thereafter to take the steps necessary to proceed with his refugee claim, he did not do so, at least until XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016. On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016. XXXX XXXX XXXX told CBSA, as interpreted, that he had not returned in XXXX 2014 to complete his refugee application because he "was unaware that a time lapse had occurred." Why then, they asked, had he not reported to any other immigration office after entering Canada to make a refugee claim? He thought the matter was over, he replied, so he had not thought he had to go to another place.3

The RPD asked XXXX XXXX XXXX when he decided to claim refugee protection in Canada. His first answer was that a friend told him in Toronto some time after his arrival there from Montreal that the fact that Canadian immigration officials had given him some papers at the airport, which he did not show the friend, meant that he could claim asylum, and that if he did so they would call him and his case would take two to three years.4 Right after that, he testified that his friend told him that perhaps he had been accepted as a refugee and they would call him.5

The RPD then asked XXXX XXXX XXXX whether CBSA was accurate that he told them on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014, the day of his arrival in Canada, that he wanted to make a refugee claim. He replied that he had not said that. They had only given him some papers and told him to leave.6

He then added that the fact that they gave him papers had made him think that "it was done, completed." The RPD then asked whether he thought he had made a refugee claim at the Montreal airport. This time he answered yes.7

CBSA's records stated that XXXX XXXX XXXX had not returned as directed to complete his refugee claim. The RPD asked why he had waited 2-1/2 years to do so. He explained that his friends told him that once his case was registered, it would take two years, not less, for them to call him.8

After that, XXXX XXXX XXXX said he had not read the notice that he would have been given before leaving the airport telling him that he had to come back and file some papers. Asked whether he had not been concerned by being in Canada for 2-1/2 years without refugee protection, he said he had understood that they gave him a paper and would call him, so he had just waited.9

Later an RPD member asked XXXX XXXX XXXX what his intent was when he left India for Canada. He thought he would be safe here from the Indian police, he replied. Asked again whether he had intended to seek refugee protection, he said the agent had told him that after entering Canada with his visa, he could consult a lawyer and make a refugee claim. Asked whether he had made a refugee claim at the airport, he said that after the officials repudiated his visa, they gave him a form and told him to go. He had thought that he had been accepted as a refugee, and he left the airport, he explained.10

Between XXXX 2014 and XXXX 2016, he then added, he had not discussed his situation with anyone, because everybody was telling him he would be called. He had not contacted a lawyer meanwhile during that period either.11 He finally did so himself in XXXX 2016, he said, because he had not been called for two years.12

Towards the end of his RPD hearing, XXXX XXXX XXXX testified that when he boarded his flight out of India, he had no plan for what he would do after arriving in Canada, because he simply had reacted to what had just happened to him with the police in India. The agent who prepared the application had told him, he said, that after entering Canada he could consult a lawyer here to be advised on his options. That that was all the agent had told him.13 Later he explained that he had eventually voluntarily contacted a Toronto lawyer because two years had gone by and he had not been called.14

Finally, Counsel asked XXXX XXXX XXXX what he had understood would happen next when he had walked out of the airport in Canada with the papers he had been given. He knew nothing, he said.15 RPD finding about delay

The RPD rejected XXXX XXXX XXXX explanations because it found it unreasonable that a person fleeing persecution would fail to have important documents, given to him by the authorities from whom he was seeking protection, translated for over two years. His failure to pursue his claim for protection for that long after reaching Canada, the RPD concluded, undermined the credibility of his allegation that he fled India because he feared persecution there.16 Appellant's position - delay Counsel submits that:
Delay in making [here: pursuing] a refugee claim is rarely grounds on its own to impugn credibility. It is an important factor but not a determinative one.

XXXX XXXX XXXX belief that there would be an over two-year delay was fairly accurate. The Auditor General has found17 that the processing time for an average refugee claim went from 19 months in 2010 to over two years in 2018.

Once the almost 2-1/2 years had passed, XXXX XXXX XXXX became proactive. He did not contact a lawyer because, say, CBSA had arrested him. He did so on his own initiative and then the process took its course.
The RPD "credibility" finding was in fact one of implausibility. It erred because such findings should only be made in the clearest of cases.

From a Canadian expert point of view, XXXX XXXX XXXX was not diligent. The RPD erred, however, by basing its finding on him not having been reasonable. First, he did not have an interpreter at the airport.18 Second, the RPD further erred by deciding the question was whether XXXX XXXX XXXX actions had been reasonable. The correct question, rather, was whether his subjective reasons for delay had a reasonable basis. That is a lower standard. The RPD erred by looking for the reasonable claimant or that person's explanation instead of analyzing whether XXXX XXXX XXXX believed what he described. Analysis - delay
I agree with Counsel's statement of the law. Applying it, however, I find that the RPD's conclusion on delay was still correct.

First, XXXX XXXX XXXX testified back and forth to two inconsistent versions of what he allegedly understood upon leaving the CBSA airport office and thereafter. In a number of instances, he claimed he believed he had been accepted as a refugee; elsewhere, that he had made a refugee claim and had to wait, probably at least two years, to be called to proceed with it. These are markedly incompatible scenarios. There could be no reasonable basis to believe both or to alternate between them.

Further, their inconsistency would have eliminated any reasonable basis for passive complacency. Given that XXXX XXXX XXXX life or at least security of the person were allegedly at risk, he would have had no reasonable basis not to seek clarification of his situation in Canada. Instead his evidence was that he neither read nor had translated to him the papers CBSA gave him, nor did he show them to anyone or seek advice from any informed source for well over two years.

Moreover, when XXXX XXXX XXXX left the airport, and for more than two years after that, he had nothing in his passport or any document giving him the right to live, work or study in Canada. According to his testimony, he had either not received or was not aware of any instructions from CBSA for how to continue his life here. That too undermines any alleged reasonable basis for believing that he could or should just wait for months on end to get on with these matters. I note here as well that XXXX XXXX XXXX had 12 years of education and had successfully established and run a business. He was not so naïve as to have a reasonable basis to believe that he should do nothing, especially given the reasons he alleged for having come to Canada.

Counsel submits that XXXX XXXX XXXX had a reasonable basis to believe that he would need to wait a good two years before his situation in Canada was resolved, because that was consistent with the average processing time for a refugee claim. That processing time, however, starts with the claimant attending a CBSA or IRCC office as directed to have the necessary forms filed or completed. It does not mean that a claimant waits two years to be called to begin to pursue their claim. The evidence does not support that being the norm or even an uncommon occurrence. In addition, given the many thousands of refugee claims made in Toronto over the years by persons who are Indian citizens or other persons of Tamil background, there would be no reasonable basis to believe, while living in that community,19 that it was.

I do not consider that XXXX XXXX XXXX apparent proactivity after 28 months outweighs the factors above. Besides those factors, he testified that the agent in India told him that after entering Canada he should consult a lawyer, variously testifying that that was to see about making a refugee claim or to find out about his immigration options generally. That being so, waiting 28 months is hardly proactive.

As a result, I conclude that the RPD did not err in finding that XXXX XXXX XXXX delay in pursuing his refugee claim undermined the credibility of his allegation that he fled India because he feared further persecution there. Given, however, that the RPD nowhere clearly rejected XXXX XXXX XXXX allegations about his interaction with police at his store in XXXX 2013, the credibility undermined was that of his subjective fear of future persecution.

Counsel is correct that delay itself is generally not determinative of overall credibility. While the delay here was substantial, I do not find that it alone was determinative of that question. Nevertheless, in my view it had a material impact. Lack of corroborating letter from the Appellant's wife - RPD correct
The RPD disbelieved that police had visited XXXX XXXX XXXX wife several times looking for him after he left India.

XXXX XXXX XXXX wrote in his BOC that after he left India, the police went to his house and threatened his wife and son. He testified that this happened in XXXX 2014, XXXX 2015, and XXXX 2017.20 He said his source of that information was telephone calls to his wife.21
The RPD found these alleged police visits not credible, because XXXX XXXX XXXX did not file a letter from his wife corroborating them.22

The RPD asked XXXX XXXX XXXX if he had asked his wife for such a letter. He said he had not. His subsequent answers indicate that he may have thought he was being asked whether he had asked her to request a letter from the police. Ultimately, however, he indicated that he did not know why he could not get (or had not got) a letter from his wife herself.23 Appellant's position - lack of corroborating letter from wife

Counsel submits that the RPD erred because XXXX XXXX XXXX was consistent in his evidence and there was no need for corroboration. He relies on a Federal Court pronouncement that where no valid reason has been provided to doubt an applicant's truthfulness, it would be an error to require corroborative evidence of such allegations as this would defeat the presumption of truthfulness.24 Analysis - lack of corroborating letter from wife

Along with the court ruling Counsel cited, refugee claims are also governed by RPD Rule 11: The claimant must provide acceptable documents establishing their identity and other elements of the claim. A claimant who does not provide acceptable documents must explain why they did not provide the documents and what steps they took to obtain them.

The reason underlying the presumption of truthfulness is that claimants who have experienced certain types of emergency situations cannot reasonably be expected to always have documents or other evidence to support their claims. However, in cases, such as XXXX XXXX XXXX, where a claimant has the opportunity to gather corroborative evidence after arriving in Canada, the strength of the presumption of truthfulness may depend directly on the extent to which corroborative evidence is provided. It follows that, if there is any reason to doubt the veracity of the allegations made in a claimant's BOC or testimony, adverse inferences about credibility may be drawn if the claimant is unable to provide a reasonable explanation for the lack of reasonably expected corroborative evidence. Similarly, where corroborative evidence should reasonably be available to establish the essential elements of a claim for refugee protection and there is no reasonable explanation for its absence, the RPD or RAD may make an adverse credibility finding based on the claimant's lack of effort to obtain such evidence.25

As found elsewhere in my reasons, the RPD had some reason besides the lack of corroboration from XXXX XXXX XXXX wife to doubt the veracity of his allegations. The RPD correctly noted that the source of XXXX XXXX XXXX information about the alleged police visits was entirely his wife. I agree with the RPD that a letter from her would have been evidence that was reasonably available, relevant, and central to a determinative issue in his case, and that he did not provide a reasonable explanation for failing to produce it.
I thus find that the RPD did not err on this point of credibility. No serious possibility police will arrest XXXX XXXX XXXX - RPD correct
The RPD found no serious possibility that the police would arrest XXXX XXXX XXXX should he return to Tamil Nadu.

In his BOC, XXXX XXXX XXXX wrote that at his shop in XXXX 2013: Police asked me lot of questions about my connection to the boys. Police accused that I was also supporting the LTTE and encouraging them. I denied but the police said that they are collecting more information and if they found out anything suspicious they will come and arrest me.26

He testified that when police asked him whether he too was connected to the LTTE, he truthfully denied it and explained he simply helped Tamils. As translated, the police then told XXXX XXXX XXXX that until they caught his other employee, XXXX XXXX XXXX would remain under their control, could not go anywhere, and would have to report to them whenever summoned.27

Asked the meaning of "not go anywhere", he explained the police instructed this would continue until they found the missing employee/LTTE supporter, and that they said XXXX XXXX XXXX was also supporting the LTTE, so until they caught the employee he could not leave the area. Asked the same question again, he said that the police told him they would be coming to question him frequently, so he should report whenever called to do so. Asked yet again to explain "can't go anywhere",28 XXXX XXXX XXXX said the police told him they suspected him, so he couldn't escape to anywhere else and would have to be available whenever police wished.29

The RPD's reasoning was that XXXX XXXX XXXX never had ties to the LTTE, there was no evidence the police might find to the contrary, and no allegation that the police had a personal vendetta against him that would make them disregard that lack of evidence.30 In its analysis, the RPD noted XXXX XXXX XXXX acknowledgment that unless the police find evidence tying him to the LTTE, they would not arrest him.31 Appellant's position - risk of arrest
Counsel submits that the RPD was wrong that XXXX XXXX XXXX was merely speculating, because:
The police had followed up and threatened his wife. [I have found, however, that the RPD correctly found this allegation not credible.]
One of his employees had been arrested and apparently had confessed to collecting funds and supporting the LTTE.

Just because XXXX XXXX XXXX said there was nothing to find tying him to the LTTE does not mean he would not be arrested. Further, the RPD erred in failing clearly to apply the correct test to the evidence, which was whether there was more than a mere possibility of persecution, not whether XXXX XXXX XXXX will be arrested.

Even if XXXX XXXX XXXX believed that if the police find nothing, they will leave him alone, the RPD ignored the documentary evidence that shows the police in India are arbitrary, non-professional and engage in torture.

The RPD was being disingenuous. The Appellant fled India because of the serious possibility that the police would return to him. The evidence shows that the rule of law in India cannot be relied on. The Appellant testified that he feared to return to India because the police were searching for him because they think he is a supporter of the LTTE. Analysis - risk of persecution - applicable test - RPD correct

Counsel argues that the RPD applied too high a test to XXXX XXXX XXXX risk of persecution by analyzing whether he will or would be arrested, and then camouflaged its error with a generic concluding sentence citing the correct test about serious possibility.32 Counsel cites jurisprudence that a correct statement of the test in conclusion does not cure the incorrect application of the test to the evidence.33

In support of his argument, Counsel highlights wording in each of the three paragraphs of the RPD's analysis on this issue. After examining those passages individually and together, I do not agree that they show that the RPD applied too high a test.

The first passage referred to XXXX XXXX XXXX agreement that it was fair to assume that if the police find nothing to tie him to the LTTE they would not arrest him.34 The proposition the RPD put to XXXX XXXX XXXX, "they will not arrest you" was that there was no chance of arrest in such circumstances. Agreeing with it meant XXXX XXXX XXXX believed that if the police found no evidence, his arrest would be a mere possibility or less. Thus, the RPD's wording here carried the opposite meaning to that which Counsel ascribes to it. It did not mean the RPD required XXXX XXXX XXXX to establish that he will be arrested should he return to India.

The second passage was the RPD's statement that "there is no evidence for the Indian police to find that would tie the claimant to the LTTE."35 The initial words "there is no evidence", however, make it clear that the RPD used "would" here in the sense of "could". Using "no evidence" to mean not enough that it will happen, though enough that it might, is an inapt construction. I do not infer it from the RPD's wording. Again, then I find that the RPD did not impose too high a test here on XXXX XXXX XXXX risk.

The third passage referred to XXXX XXXX XXXX "assertion that the police will come and arrest him". The RPD found this was based on mere speculation and not to constitute credible evidence of future risk. The RPD then concluded that, "There is no serious possibility that the police will arrest and detain the claimant."

XXXX XXXX XXXX only said "will arrest" or words to that effect twice in the two hours of his RPD hearing. The first was when he testified that the police told his wife after he left India that they "will arrest him" when he comes back "if the evidence is proven" (as translated).36 The other was when he was asked what he has to be afraid of if there is no information inculpating him. He replied that he would still not be safe because for certain, even if not for the employee/LTTE case, the police might suspect him in some other case "and they will arrest me."37 Elsewhere he used words speaking not of "will", but of doubt or little chance that he would be safe.38

So, the RPD may have overstated XXXX XXXX XXXX overall description of his risk. Nevertheless, I do not agree with counsel that their correct phrasing of the applicable test, right after the passage in question, was too little too late. Their use of "will" here referred only to XXXX XXXX XXXX testimony. It was not an expression of a test. The only application of the test came in the RPD's concluding sentence. The RPD put the test correctly.
I thus conclude that the RPD did not err throughout its analysis in expressing or indicating the correct test of future risk. Analysis - risk of persecution - Appellant's own evidence

That in itself is not determinative of this appeal. I must, of course, independently analyze the evidence of XXXX XXXX XXXX risk of future persecution in India and decide whether the RPD's conclusion was correct both in form and substance. To recall, the context is that the RPD accepted that XXXX XXXX XXXX allegations about his experiences with the police in 2013 were credible, but found correctly that his allegations that the police harassed his wife after he left were not.

The RPD held that XXXX XXXX XXXX did not have a well-founded fear of persecution because, it found, he never associated with the LTTE, did not know of anything the police could find to the contrary, acknowledged that if they did not they would not arrest him, and there was no allegation of a police personal vendetta against him. The RPD concluded that XXXX XXXX XXXX alleged fear of future persecution was purely speculative and that there was no serious possibility that police would come after him.39 Appellant's position - risk of persecution - Appellant's own evidence

Counsel submits that the RPD failed to consider the documentary evidence. He cites the US Department of State's reference to reports of arbitrary killings; forced disappearance; torture; rape in police custody; arbitrary arrest and detention; harsh and life-threatening prison conditions; as well as reports of political prisoners in certain [unspecified] states. This evidence, he maintains, shows that the rule of law in India cannot be relied on.40

Counsel also highlights evidence that India has not ratified the Convention Against Torture, that in a recent year 894 deaths in judicial custody and 74 in police custody were recorded, as well as 1,680 between April 2017 and February 2018. That there are credible reports of police torture, fatal beatings and rape, including of men, that prison conditions were often life-threatening or otherwise terrible, and that judicial corruption is widespread and the judicial system seriously overburdened and delayed.41 Analysis - risk of persecution - Appellant's own evidence
Credible and disturbing as that evidence is, the RPD based its decision on the risk that the Tamil Nadu state police, the force in question, would arrest XXXX XXXX XXXX in the first place.

According to the evidence, the police took immediate aggressive action against XXXX XXXX XXXX employees, arresting one and searching for the other. They took no such action against him. They did not arbitrarily detain or assault him. He testified that after officers questioned him at his store in XXXX 2013, he did not see or hear from them again before he left India four months later,42 albeit he went to live at a friend's house in Chennai; more importantly, there was no evidence police had gone to his house during that period or had tried to summon him. There was also no credible evidence, and no evidence at all in the affidavits of a friend and of a business colleague, that police had summoned or come after XXXX XXXX XXXX in the well over five years since he left India.

In these circumstances, and even having accepted as credible, as the RPD did, XXXX XXXX XXXX allegations of his experience with the police in XXXX 2013, I agree with the RPD, subject to my consideration below of the two affidavits he filed, that he had not established by his own evidence a well-founded fear of persecution should he now return to India. Affidavits - RPD partially incorrect, but result correct

XXXX XXXX XXXX filed XXXX 2018 affidavits from a friend and from a fellow spare parts retailer. The friend corroborated XXXX XXXX XXXX compassion for Tamil refugees and his having employed two of them. It added that he had "problems because of them" and that police arrested one whom they accused of Tiger connections. Finally, it stated that XXXX XXXX XXXX was "also branded as Tiger supporter as he helped them."43

The retailer described his close knowledge of XXXX XXXX XXXX and his business, with which he frequently dealt. He corroborated his employment of the two Tamil youths. He then stated that J was arrested in 2013 while collecting money for the Tigers, was beaten and he confessed, but that K hid. It adds that XXXX XXXX XXXX was questioned by police and accused of also helping the Tigers, and that "the inquiry continued". This led to the store being closed and XXXX XXXX XXXX approaching politicians for help. The affiant explains that XXXX XXXX XXXX shared his difficulties with him and asked him to buy his stock to help him reach safety, which he did. He concludes by saying that if XXXX XXXX XXXX "is here he will be accused with unrelated offences and sent to jail."44

As to the affidavits, the RPD gave them no weight on the "determinative issues" of XXXX XXXX XXXX subjective fear of persecution and his risk of future persecution. Regarding the friend's assertion that XXXX XXXX XXXX was branded a Tiger supporter, the RPD remarked that the affiant did not say by whom, nor how he knows this.45

As for the retailer's affidavit, the RPD found its assertion that were XXXX XXXX XXXX back home he would be charged with unrelated offences "inconsistent with the evidence of the claimant who has said nothing about the possibility of being charged with unrelated offences."46 That is wrong. XXXX XXXX XXXX testified that he risked that very thing.47
The RPD also observed that the retailer had not given the source of his information.48 Not quite: The affiant said XXXX XXXX XXXX shared his difficulties with him.

The RPD noted that XXXX XXXX XXXX had been unable to say when the affidavits were requested, what information their authors had been given, and what they had been asked to convey; it was another friend, the one with whom XXXX XXXX XXXX testified he stayed for four months before leaving India, who had asked the authors to write them, and not the claimant.49 Affidavits - Appellant's position

Counsel argues that the RPO erred in giving no weight to the affidavits. Despite their frailties, he submits, they confirm that XXXX XXXX XXXX had problems with the police because of the Tamil employees.50 Affidavits - analysis

I agree with the RPD that the affidavits do not outweigh its concerns, at least as far as XXXX XXXX XXXX subjective fear of persecution or the finding that he had not established a well-founded fear of future persecution.

Regarding the retailer's affidavit, in my opinion, the RPD's analysis contains two errors. The first was the factual one I mentioned above concerning its supposed inconsistency about the possibility of unrelated offences. The second was its complaint that another friend communicated with the authors rather than the Appellant doing so, and that XXXX XXXX XXXX could not say when, what information the authors had been given or what they had been asked to convey. I fail to see how that diminishes their authenticity or weight. One might imagine, if a touch cynically, that had XXXX XXXX XXXX said he gave the authors information and asked them to convey certain things that might have been held against him too. The RPD's complaint does not diminish the affidavits' independence.
The second error applies equally to the friend's affidavit.

Nevertheless, in my opinion, the affidavits, individually or together, do not merit sufficient weight to counterbalance the RPD's otherwise correct findings against XXXX XXXX XXXX subjective fear and risk of future persecution. Neither of them speaks to, let alone clears up, the problems I set out above on those questions.51 They provide nothing to explain XXXX XXXX XXXX long delay in pursuing his refugee claim. They contain no evidence of any police interest or follow up after police questioned XXXX XXXX XXXX at his shop in XXXX 2013.

Finally, the assertions the affidavits contain that XXXX XXXX XXXX was perceived as a Tiger supporter appear simply to have been conveyed to their authors by XXXX XXXX XXXX himself. While that is not necessarily a fatal defect in itself, the point here is that the authors convey no information that he has been so labelled after XXXX 2013 and particularly by the police.

I thus conclude that the RPD did not err in the outcome of its weighing of the affidavits. It follows that my findings above that were subject to consideration of the affidavits have become conclusive. Conclusion

I conclude that the RPD was correct to determine that XXXX XXXX XXXX had not established a well-founded fear of persecution. My findings above mean that the RPD also did not err in holding that XXXX XXXX XXXX did not meet the requirements for protection under IRPA section 97.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant XXXX XXXX is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
